1.pericope_label: Moreover take thou up a lamentation for the princes of Israel, And say, What is thy mother? A lioness: she lay down among lions, she nourished her whelps among young lions. And she brought up one of her whelps: it became a young lion, and it learned to catch the prey; it devoured men. The nations also heard of him; he was taken in their pit, and they brought him with chains unto the land of Egypt.

schools.summary: Summarise the parable as a whole and make the mother the national community, noting the lion figure's currency in Scripture and in Babylonia.
Read the parable as an assignment of blame the people will not accept, and take the lying among lions as moral assimilation to the Gentiles.
Set out the two parables and their referents, and take the lying among lions for confederacy with neighbouring kings.
Locates the grief in the eclipse of the covenant with David, and draws from the commission that a minister who foretells destruction must also lament it.

debates.question: Who is the mother of the princes?

positions.position: The whole body of the people, not the royal house only nor the city, as the Targum's congregation of Israel.
The whole national community, the theocracy, represented since the captivity of the ten tribes by Judah.
The land of Judea, the chief city, and the royal family of David together.
Judea is the mother and Jerusalem the lioness.

debates.question: What does lying down among lions mean?

positions.position: Confederacy and familiarity with the neighbouring kings, lion here meaning king.
A shameful mixture with the corruption of the Gentiles, contrary to the very condition on which they were chosen.

outliers.claim: Explains the pit from the practice of huntsmen who surround a portion of forest and narrow the enclosure until the beasts tread on pits lightly covered with branches and turf.
Notes that the word rendered chains is literally nose-rings, which keeps up the figure of the lion, and that the opening clause alludes to assembling the neighbourhood to secure such a beast.

themes: Moreover take thou up a lamentation for the princes of Israel,
And say, What is thy mother? A lioness: she lay down among lions, she nourished her whelps among young lions.
And she brought up one of her whelps: it became a young lion, and it learned to catch the prey; it devoured men.
The nations also heard of him; he was taken in their pit, and they brought him with chains unto the land of Egypt.

5.pericope_label: Now when she saw that she had waited, and her hope was lost, then she took another of her whelps, and made him a young lion. And he went up and down among the lions, he became a young lion, and learned to catch the prey, and devoured men. And he knew their desolate palaces, and he laid waste their cities; and the land was desolate, and the fulness thereof, by the noise of his roaring. Then the nations set against him on every side from the provinces, and spread their net over him: he was taken in their pit. And they put him in ward in chains, and brought him to the king of Babylon: they brought him into holds, that his voice should no more be heard upon the mountains of Israel.

schools.summary: Argues from the manner of each king's death that the second whelp must be Jehoiachin, and corrects the desolate palaces to widows.
Identify the second king as Jehoiakim, set up by conquest, and weigh two senses of the verb by which the nations moved against him.
Name the same king, contrast his eleven years with his brother's three months, and keep the palaces against the marginal widows.

debates.question: Which king is the second whelp?

positions.position: Jehoiakim, set up by the conqueror and carried away for his perfidy.
Jehoiachin, since Jehoiakim died in disgrace at Jerusalem and was succeeded by his son without foreign interference.

debates.question: Should the clause read desolate palaces or widows?

positions.position: Widows: the word should be so rendered, and the king's violation of them is an unavoidable departure from the figure.
Reports the widows reading beside the received one, taking them for women he had widowed by slaying their husbands for their substance.
Keeps the palaces, which he came to know by taking them and made desolate.

outliers.claim: Takes the going up and down among lions to describe the manner rather than the length of the reign, since kings in those regions were then scarcely human and everywhere like lions, so that this one was their ally in ferocity.
Explains the mother's waiting by sheer weakness, the Jews finding they could not resist with any hope of success, so that the king of Egypt was permitted to do as he pleased.

themes: Now when she saw that she had waited, and her hope was lost, then she took another of her whelps, and made him a young lion.
And he went up and down among the lions, he became a young lion, and learned to catch the prey, and devoured men.
And he knew their desolate palaces, and he laid waste their cities; and the land was desolate, and the fulness thereof, by the noise of his roaring.
Then the nations set against him on every side from the provinces, and spread their net over him: he was taken in their pit.
And they put him in ward in chains, and brought him to the king of Babylon: they brought him into holds, that his voice should no more be heard upon the mountains of Israel.

10.pericope_label: Thy mother is like a vine in thy blood, planted by the waters: she was fruitful and full of branches by reason of many waters. And she had strong rods for the sceptres of them that bare rule, and her stature was exalted among the thick branches, and she appeared in her height with the multitude of her branches.

schools.summary: Correct thick branches to clouds as deliberate hyperbole, and either read the obscure phrase as the vine living in the life of her children or avoid it by rendering the word repose.
Set the nation's former dignity against its present misery, and insist the sceptres were gathered from these very branches rather than exceeded by them.
Explain the blood from vine husbandry or from the royal line, and read the fruitfulness as children and able men.
Develops the vine set in blood into an observation that places of great wickedness may prosper for a while, and makes the strong rods the magistrates.

debates.question: What does the phrase in thy blood mean?

positions.position: Confesses he knows not what to make of it, and lays out three proposals: the blood of the grape, an emendation to at a pomegranate, and a one-letter change giving thy vineyard.
If the text stands, a vine living in the blood, that is the life, of her children.
An allusion to laying blood at the roots of vines to make them fruitful, applied to the royal blood.
Avoids the difficulty by rendering the word repose: planted by the water in thy repose.
The many able men who rose in the nation and were fit to hold sceptres.
The magistrates, men of sense and experience, branches of uncommon strength or poles for the vine's support.
Zedekiah and his many sons, whose number fed the pride that persuaded him he might safely rebel.
The branches from which the sceptres were gathered, kings being taken from the people as branches from a vine.

outliers.claim: Uses the change of figure to set the nation's two states side by side, since they had grown callous and would not look back, remaining as wanton as in prosperity when scarcely anything was left safe but Jerusalem.
Insists this is not the vine of low stature of the earlier parable but a strong and goodly vine, and corrects thick branches to clouds as hyperbole for its excellence.

themes: Thy mother is like a vine in thy blood, planted by the waters: she was fruitful and full of branches by reason of many waters.
And she had strong rods for the sceptres of them that bare rule, and her stature was exalted among the thick branches, and she appeared in her height with the multitude of her branches.

12.pericope_label: But she was plucked up in fury, she was cast down to the ground, and the east wind dried up her fruit: her strong rods were broken and withered; the fire consumed them. And now she is planted in the wilderness, in a dry and thirsty ground. And fire is gone out of a rod of her branches, which hath devoured her fruit, so that she hath no strong rod to be a sceptre to rule. This is a lamentation, and shall be for a lamentation.

schools.summary: Dates the desolation from the earlier captivity and reads the past tense as prophetic sight, then extends the wilderness past the return to a discipline preparing a few for a kingdom not of this world.
Explain the suddenness as what strikes men to the quick, meet the objection that a burnt vine cannot be replanted, and lay the last slaughter on the people themselves.
Fill the clauses with the events of the siege and the blinding, and dispute whose rod it was that the fire came out of.

debates.question: Whose rod is the fire that devoured her fruit?

positions.position: Zedekiah, the fire being his rebellion and the breaking of his covenant and oath.
Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, also of the blood-royal, who assassinated the governor and carried off the people.
The people themselves, the image showing that the last slaughter proceeded from them and forestalling their complaints.

outliers.claim: Raises against himself the objection that a vine described as withered and burnt cannot also be planted in a desert, and answers that the burning states the conclusion men's senses were bound to reach when the city was ruined, not the final state of the thing.

Reads the dry ground past the exile itself, holding that the Jews never again rose to importance among the nations but were meanwhile disciplined so that a few might be prepared for a kingdom not of this world.

themes: But she was plucked up in fury, she was cast down to the ground, and the east wind dried up her fruit: her strong rods were broken and withered; the fire consumed them.
And now she is planted in the wilderness, in a dry and thirsty ground.
And fire is gone out of a rod of her branches, which hath devoured her fruit, so that she hath no strong rod to be a sceptre to rule. This is a lamentation, and shall be for a lamentation.
